Summary:

Maximova et al. report on studies using a non-human primate model of encephalitis due to West Nile virus (WNV). WNV is the leading cause of arboviral neuroinvasive disease in the US with post-infectious neurologic sequelae including movement disorders and memory impairments. The authors performed intracerebral inoculation of a virulent strain of WNV and performed extensive analyses of WNV-induced alterations in gene expression on cerebellar and spinal cord tissues at 3, 7, and 9 days post-infection (dpi) compared with mock-infected animals. They also performed immunohistochemical studies examining astrocytes, microglia and T cells and neuronal infection, loss and synapse elimination.

The paper is very well-written, supports findings in murine models and human disease, which have shown that presynaptic termini are eliminated in the WNV-infected hippocampus. That these processes may occur in multiple CNS regions is clinically relevant and supports the need for translation of these findings into new targets that might address multiple neurologic symptoms and sequelae.

This is a largely descriptive study on the transcriptional response of two brain regions, the cerebellum and spinal cord, to i.c.v. infusion of West Nile virus. The strength of the study is the use of non-human primates, analysis at two time-points post infection and the importance of the topic in light of the current global viral pandemic. Analytics that focus on particular cellular components, thereby identifying genes associated with pre- and post-synaptic compartments as particularly strongly regulated targets, is another strength. The use of IHC to confirm predicted changes in protein levels under girding astrocytosis, microglia and T-cell reactivity and cell death is a further strength.

Essential revisions:

1) It is important to remember that WNV only causes disease in NHPs when the virus is directly inoculated into the brain (as pointed out by the authors). This raises important questions about the contribution of putting a needle directly in the brain and how this affects gene regulation. Unfortunately, the authors do not tell us if the control animals also received a needle injection into the brain too (nor does Maximova et al., 2014, the original study). This is an important point to consider in terms of the validity of the data. It is interesting that changes were detected in the spinal cord before the cerebellum in virus infected animals plus no gene changes in the cerebellum at day 3pi supporting the possibility that the needle injection does not contribute to the data obtained. However, this needs to be formally addressed in the revision.

2) Related to the above, there is limited information as to how well the i.c.v. infusion of virus replicates WNV-ND in humans and this too should be more formally addressed. The Discussion provides a justification for the system being used. The reviewers note this is an artificial system. Humans get WN disease following a mosquito bite and the virus crosses the periphery into the brain. Humans do not get the virus infection by direct injection into the brain. I think this paragraph needs some revisions.

3) The manuscript would benefit from more cellular analyses to localize synaptic proteins within microglia or astrocytes within the CB and SC, and their relationship with clinical findings. Presumably the authors have existing tissue which could be further analyzed to address, at least in part, some of the following issues:

a) Figure 4. The authors show extensive astrocyte and microglial activation in both CNS regions of infected NHPs. Given the microglial nodules observed, can they also determine whether there was any observed neuronophagia in these tissues?

b) Figure 5. The loss of synaptophysin is very striking. Can the authors also look at post-synaptic markers to determine whether both sides of the synapse are affected? It would also be important to determine whether synaptic elements can be detected within microglia, as has been observed in murine models of WNV CNS infection.

c) Figure 6. The data demonstrating differential regulation of pre- and post-synaptic genes is very striking. As mRNAs for synaptic genes are localized in neurites, it would be important to determine whether the pre-synaptic termini are eliminated more efficiently and the post-synaptic termini spared.

d) Figure 7. As a follow-up, it would be important to examine locations of synapse elimination within both CNS regions and relate this to motor findings in the animals.

Also, given the role of IL-1 in neurotoxicity (shown in both in vitro and WNV models; 10.1038/nature21029 and 10.1038/s41590-017-0021-y), it would be interesting to determine cellular sources of this cytokine in the NHP model.

4) Figure 1. The authors mention that animals are euthanized when they develop severe neurologic symptoms. Please comment on whether the model would lead to universal death in NHPs if this were not performed. This is important because it is unclear whether patient survivors exhibit the same loss of neurons observed in those who succumb during acute CNS infection. Can the authors report on whether expression of the same genes is altered in both CNS regions during symptomatic stages of disease? Also, as many genes designated as “immune systems” function in the CNS during development and repair, it would be important to categorize them as “ׅneuroimmune systems”, which is consistent with increasing evidence of ancestral functions of neural genes as immune genes. It would also be helpful to highlight those known to function during development as they may be involved in repair.

5) Figure 2. This figure shows upregulated immune system genes and down-regulated nervous system genes. It would be important to look at both up and down in both systems for the two regions. It is interesting that the CB seems to lag behind the spinal cord with regard to innate immune responses such as activation of TLRs. Can the authors comment on the time-frame of appearance of symptoms in the animals? That is, do spinal cord deficits precede cerebellar deficits? It also appears that cytokine signaling is quite different between the two regions. Studies in mice suggest that the CB is far less targeted by WNV and has constitutive expression of many PRRs. Is this the case in NHPs?

6) Figure 3. The results of these analyses are consistent with published studies showing persistent activation of innate and adaptive immune responses after viral clearance. The more subtle changes in nervous system genes are also consistent with results suggesting that survivors of WNV may not have extensive neural cell damage but instead exhibit alterations in neuronal networks. Can the authors provide any additional analyses to evaluate this such as examining cell death pathways in neurons?

7) That the genes which are being regulated have multiple functions, i.e. are pleiotropic, does not seem particularly surprising. The authors argue this leads to unintended deleterious effects but the logical connection there is not clear, why could it not be the opposite? Actually providing a benefit?

claims.claim: In the spinal cord at 3 dpi, six genes were significantly upregulated: MX1, IFIT3, IFI44L, PARP9, STAT1, and TRIM22.
claims.source: In the spinal cord, however, six genes were significantly upregulated (FDR < 0.05; fold change ≥2 over mock) and none were significantly downregulated. claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology annotation analysis of the upregulated genes.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescent staining data and visualization in Figure 7d.

claims.claim: Focal accumulations of WNV+++ granules in the proximal dendrites of SMNs could be seen immediately adjacent to the remaining ChAT+ cholinergic presynaptic C-boutons, suggesting trans-synaptic spread and/or local postsynaptic replication of WNV.
claims.source: Interestingly, focal accumulations of WNV+++ granules in the proximal dendrites of SMNs (postsynaptic sites) could be seen immediately adjacent to the remaining ChAT+ cholinergic presynaptic C-boutons, suggesting trans-synaptic spread and/or local postsynaptic replication of WNV (Figure 7d, WNV+++/ChAT+ SMN).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescent staining data and visualization in Figure 7d, with an inference about viral spread mechanisms.

claims.claim: Immunoreactivity for synaptophysin (SYP) was greatly depleted in advanced WNV-ND compared to mock, encompassing all layers of the cerebellar cortex and gray matter of the spinal cord.
claims.source: Immunoreactivity for the synaptic marker protein synaptophysin (SYP) was greatly depleted in advanced WNV-ND compared to mock, encompassing all layers of the cerebellar cortex (i.e., molecular layer, Purkinje cell layer, and granule cell layer) (Figure 8a) and gray matter of the spinal cord (Figure 8c).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data and visualization in Figures 8a and 8c.

claims.claim: Immunoreactivity for MAP2 was markedly reduced, confirming the loss of neuronal somatodendritic integrity in Purkinje cells and granule cells in the cerebellum and spinal motor neurons in the ventral horns of the spinal cord.
claims.source: Immunoreactivity for microtubule-associated protein 2 (MAP2, a marker for somatodendritic [and thus, postsynaptic] compartments of neurons) was also markedly reduced, confirming the loss of neuronal somatodendritic integrity in Purkinje cells and granule cells in the cerebellum (Figure 8b) and spinal motor neurons in the ventral horns of the spinal cord (Figure 8d).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data and visualization in Figures 8b and 8d.

claims.claim: The synapse was identified as the most significantly dysregulated neuronal cell compartment in advanced WNV-ND.
claims.source: Ranking the neuronal CC GO terms based on their enrichment values, we identified the synapse as the most significantly dysregulated neuronal cell compartment (Figure 8e and f; note the smallest FDR value for the GO CC term synapse (GO:0045202)).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis and visualization in Figures 8e and 8f.

claims.claim: The spinal cord had about 2.5 times more dysregulated genes annotated to the GO CC term synapse compared to the cerebellum.
claims.source: This phenomenon was observed in both the cerebellum and spinal cord, albeit the spinal cord had about 2.5 times more dysregulated genes annotated to the GO CC term synapse compared to the cerebellum.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparative analysis of gene ontology enrichment data.

claims.claim: Glutamatergic (i.e., asymmetric, axo-dendritic, and excitatory) synapses and GABA-ergic (i.e., symmetric, axo-somatic, and inhibitory) synapses emerged as significantly transcriptionally dysregulated in both the cerebellum and spinal cord.
claims.source: Further defining the types of synapses affected in WNV-ND, glutamatergic (i.e., asymmetric, axo-dendritic, and excitatory) synapses (GO:0098978) and GABA-ergic (i.e., symmetric, axo-somatic, and inhibitory) synapses (GO:0098982) emerged as significantly transcriptionally dysregulated in both the cerebellum and spinal cord (Figure 8e and f).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis and visualization in Figures 8e and 8f.

claims.claim: In the cerebellum, the postsynapse was the most significantly affected synaptic subcompartment based on the lowest Q-value.
claims.source: In the cerebellum, the postsynapse was the most significantly affected synaptic subcompartment based on the lowest Q-value (Figure 9c; Table 2), followed by the presynapse and synaptic cleft, while the most affected synaptic functions were the synapse organization (regulation of synapse assembly/synapse adhesion between pre- and postsynapse), trans-synaptic signaling (modulation of chemical synaptic transmission), processes in presynapse (synaptic vesicle cycle), and processes in postsynapse (regulation of postsynaptic membrane potential/neurotransmitter receptor levels) (Figure 9d; Table 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by SynGO enrichment analysis and visualization in Figure 9c and Table 2.

claims.claim: Compared to the cerebellum, the spinal cord had many more synaptic locations and functions affected and more enriched.
claims.source: Compared to the cerebellum, the spinal cord had many more synaptic locations (Figure 9e; Table 2) and functions (Figure 9f; Table 2) affected and more enriched (including many sublocations and specific synaptic functions).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by SynGO enrichment analysis and visualization in Figures 9e, 9f, and Table 2.

claims.claim: At the early-symptomatic stage of WNV-ND, 80% of synaptic genes in the cerebellum were upregulated and 20% were downregulated.
claims.source: Analysis of upregulated versus downregulated synaptic genes in the cerebellum at the early-symptomatic stage of WNV-ND showed that 80% of synaptic genes were upregulated and 20% were downregulated (Table 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by SynGO enrichment analysis and data in Table 3.

claims.claim: The upregulated synaptic genes in the cerebellum at the early-symptomatic stage were postsynaptic while the downregulated genes were presynaptic.
claims.source: The upregulated synaptic genes were postsynaptic while the downregulated genes were presynaptic.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by SynGO enrichment analysis of synaptic genes.

claims.claim: Transcriptional regulation in the spinal cord at the early-symptomatic stage of WNV-ND was characterized by a similar number of upregulated (51.2%) and downregulated (48.8%) synaptic genes.
claims.source: Transcriptional regulation in the spinal cord at this early-symptomatic stage of WNV-ND was characterized by a similar number of upregulated (51.2%) and downregulated (48.8%) synaptic genes, which were annotated to both the presynapse and postsynapse and had functions in synapse organization and chemical synaptic transmission (Table 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by SynGO enrichment analysis and data in Table 3.

claims.claim: At the advanced-symptomatic stage of WNV-ND, the number of downregulated synaptic genes increased relative to upregulated genes in both the cerebellum and spinal cord, with a higher percentage of downregulated genes in the spinal cord (71.5%).
claims.source: At the advanced-symptomatic stage of WNV-ND, the number of downregulated synaptic genes increased relative to upregulated genes in both the cerebellum and spinal cord, with a higher percentage of downregulated genes in the spinal cord (71.5%).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by SynGO enrichment analysis of synaptic genes at the advanced-symptomatic stage.

claims.claim: About one third of the differentially expressed synaptic genes were upregulated at the advanced-symptomatic stage in both the cerebellum and spinal cord (45.9% and 28.5%, respectively).
claims.source: Nonetheless, about one third of the differentially expressed synaptic genes were upregulated at this stage in both the cerebellum and spinal cord (45.9% and 28.5%, respectively).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by SynGO enrichment analysis of synaptic genes at the advanced-symptomatic stage.

claims.claim: Relative to the total number of WNV-induced DEGs, the cerebellum had a higher percentage of immune DEGs (33.1%), compared to the spinal cord (18.6%).
claims.source: Relative to the total number of WNV-induced DEGs, the cerebellum had a higher percentage of immune DEGs (33.1%), compared to the spinal cord (18.6%), even though the absolute number of immune DEGs in the spinal cord was higher.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of immune and neural DEGs and their distribution.

claims.claim: Despite more than twice the number of the neural DEGs induced in the spinal cord compared to the cerebellum (642 vs. 252), the percentage of neural DEGs relative to the total number of DEGs was almost identical in these two CNS structures (14.6% vs. 14.5%).
claims.source: Strikingly, despite more than twice the number of the neural DEGs induced in the spinal cord compared to the cerebellum (642 vs. 252), the percentage of neural DEGs relative to the total number of DEGs was almost identical in these two CNS structures (14.6% vs. 14.5%) (Figure 10a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of immune and neural DEGs and visualization in Figure 10a.

claims.claim: 94 and 179 common immune-neural DEGs were induced in the cerebellum and spinal cord, respectively, indicating that these DEGs have a dual immune-neural functionality, suggesting that they are pleiotropic.
claims.source: We next identified 94 and 179 common immune-neural DEGs that were induced in the cerebellum and spinal cord, respectively (Figure 10a). This indicates that these DEGs have a dual immune-neural functionality, suggesting that they are pleiotropic (Radisky et al., 2009; Boulanger, 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis and visualization in Figure 10a, with citations supporting the concept of pleiotropy.

claims.claim: Somatodendritic compartment, neuron projection, and synapse were identified as the main neuronal targets of regulation by pleiotropic genes.
claims.source: We next asked what neuronal locations and functions were under transcriptional control by the WNV-induced pleiotropic genes. Somatodendritic compartment, neuron projection, and synapse were identified as the main neuronal targets of regulation by pleiotropic genes (ORT; CC GO domain; FDR < 0.05) (Table 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by overrepresentation test analysis and data in Table 4.

claims.claim: Neuron projection development, regulation of the neuron death, microglial/astroglial cell activation/migration, axon guidance, synapse structure/activity, postsynapse to nucleus signaling, and synapse pruning were identified as the main functions regulated by pleiotropic genes.
claims.source: Neuron projection development, regulation of the neuron death, microglial/astroglial cell activation/migration, axon guidance, synapse structure/activity, postsynapse to nucleus signaling, and synapse pruning were identified as the main functions regulated by pleiotropic genes (ORT; BP GO domain; FDR < 0.05) (Table 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by overrepresentation test analysis and data in Table 4.

claims.claim: A Venn diagram comparison identified an overlap containing 36 immune-neural-synaptic pleiotropic DEGs, of which 19 were upregulated and 17 were downregulated.
claims.source: A Venn diagram comparison identified an overlap containing 36 immune-neural-synaptic pleiotropic DEGs, of which 19 were upregulated and 17 were downregulated (Figure 9b; Supplementary file 7, 'Immune-neural-synaptic pleiotropic genes').
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis and visualization in Figure 9b.

claims.claim: The gene C1QA that encodes a major constituent of the complement system subcomponent C1 was upregulated and mapped to significantly enriched GO terms associated with immune/defense response to virus infection, glial cell response, neuron differentiation, and synapse, as well as synaptic pruning.
claims.source: Interestingly, interrogation of specific pleiotropic genes showed that the gene C1QA that encodes a major constituent of the complement system subcomponent C1, was upregulated and mapped to significantly enriched GO terms associated with (i) immune/defense response to virus infection, (ii) glial cell response, (iii) neuron differentiation, and (iv) synapse (Supplementary file 8, gProfiler: Immune-neural-synaptic pleiotropic DEGs'), as well as synaptic pruning (Table 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis and data in Table 4 and Supplementary file 8.

claims.claim: Both up- and downregulated pleiotropic genes had functionality in synapse organization and topology at the presynapse and postsynapse.
claims.source: Since the synapse emerged as the neuronal cell compartment most significantly enriched for pleiotropic genes (Figure 10c–f), we applied synaptic GO enrichment analysis (SynGO) and found that both up- and downregulated genes had functionality in synapse organization and topology (i.e., localization of the gene product functions) at the presynapse and postsynapse (Figure 10g).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by SynGO enrichment analysis and visualization in Figure 10g.

claims.claim: The GO term of chemical synaptic transmission was significantly enriched for upregulated pleiotropic genes.
claims.source: Specifically, the GO term of chemical synaptic transmission was significantly enriched for upregulated pleiotropic genes, while the GO term of protein catabolic process at the postsynapse was significantly enriched for downregulated pleiotropic genes (Figure 10g).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by SynGO enrichment analysis and visualization in Figure 10g.

claims.claim: The GO term of protein catabolic process at the postsynapse was significantly enriched for downregulated pleiotropic genes.
claims.source: Specifically, the GO term of chemical synaptic transmission was significantly enriched for upregulated pleiotropic genes, while the GO term of protein catabolic process at the postsynapse was significantly enriched for downregulated pleiotropic genes (Figure 10g).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by SynGO enrichment analysis and visualization in Figure 10g.

claims.claim: qPCR analysis of select transcripts confirmed their significant dysregulation during WNV infection in the cerebella of NHPs.
claims.source: qPCR analysis of these select transcripts had confirmed their significant (one-way ANOVA; p<0.05) dysregulation during WNV infection in the cerebella of NHPs (Supplementary file 10, 'WNV-ND transcriptome validation').
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR validation data in Supplementary file 10.

claims.claim: A linear regression analysis returned strong and significant correlations between the expression values for select genes as determined by microarray or qPCR at the symptomatic stages of WNV-ND.
claims.source: In addition, a linear regression analysis returned the strong and significant correlations between the expression values for these select genes as determined by microarray or qPCR at the symptomatic stages of WNV-ND (early-symptomatic stage: R2 = 0.998, p<0.05; advanced-symptomatic stage: R2 = 0.987, p<0.05).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by linear regression analysis of microarray and qPCR data.

claims.claim: WNV infection disrupts the homeostasis of the immune-neural-synaptic axis via induction of pleiotropic genes with distinct functions in each component of the axis.
claims.source: By examining the regulation of the immune and nervous system processes in a nonhuman primate model of West Nile virus neurological disease, we show that virus infection disrupts the homeostasis of the immune-neural-synaptic axis via induction of pleiotropic genes with distinct functions in each component of the axis.
claims.evidence: The claim is a major conclusion of the study based on multiple lines of experimental evidence presented throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: This pleiotropic gene regulation suggests an unintended off-target negative impact of virus-induced host immune responses on the neurotransmission.
claims.source: This pleiotropic gene regulation suggests an unintended off-target negative impact of virus-induced host immune responses on the neurotransmission, which may be a common feature of various viral infections of the CNS.
claims.evidence: The claim is a major conclusion of the study based on inference from the experimental data on pleiotropic gene regulation.

claims.claim: Many viruses can invade the central nervous system (CNS), infect the neurons, propagate by exploiting cellular machinery, hijack axonal transport, and cross the synapses to disseminate within neural networks.
claims.source: Many viruses can invade the central nervous system (CNS), infect the neurons, propagate by exploiting cellular machinery, hijack axonal transport, and cross the synapses to disseminate within neural networks (Taylor and Enquist, 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Taylor and Enquist, 2015, which provides published evidence for viral mechanisms of CNS invasion.

claims.claim: WNV can infect the CNS, use bi-directional axonal transport, and spread trans-synaptically.
claims.source: This is also true for the West Nile virus (WNV), which can infect the CNS, use bi-directional axonal transport, and spread trans-synaptically (Maximova et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Maximova et al., 2016, which provides published evidence for WNV mechanisms of CNS infection and spread.

claims.claim: Postulated mechanisms of the neuropathogenic impact of WNV infection center around the loss of neurons due to either direct cytopathic effect of virus replication or damaging effects of the inflammatory environment developing in response to infection.
claims.source: Postulated mechanisms of the neuropathogenic impact of WNV infection center around the loss of neurons due to either direct cytopathic effect of virus replication or damaging effects of the inflammatory environment developing in response to infection.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about proposed mechanisms of WNV neuropathogenesis.

claims.claim: Several studies have provided insights into changes in gene expression in the CNS after an experimental WNV infection, mainly focused on the immune responses and apoptosis.
claims.source: Although several studies have provided insights into changes in gene expression in the CNS after an experimental WNV infection, they mainly focused on the immune responses and apoptosis (Lim et al., 2017; Kosch et al., 2018; Bourgeois et al., 2011; Clarke et al., 2014a; Venter et al., 2005; Green et al., 2016; Kumar et al., 2016; Clarke et al., 2014b; Vig et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies that have examined gene expression changes in WNV infection.

claims.claim: The kinetics of viral replication in the cerebellum and lumbar spinal cord were very similar.
claims.source: However, the kinetics of viral replication in the cerebellum and lumbar spinal cord were very similar (1.8 ± 0.2 and <1.7 log10PFU/g [at or below the limit of detection] at 3 dpi; 6.4 ± 0.3 and 5.6 ± 0.4 log10PFU/g at 7 dpi; and 6.9 ± 0.1 and 5.8 ± 0.2 log10PFU/g at 9 dpi, respectively) (Maximova et al., 2016; Maximova et al., 2014), suggesting that the virus had an equal opportunity to infect respective target neurons and to use their cellular machinery to establish productive replication.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by viral titer data from previous studies (Maximova et al., 2016; Maximova et al., 2014).

claims.claim: CNS-site-specificity in immune responses to viral infections and in mechanisms of the non-cytolytic clearance of the virus from non-renewable neurons by T and B cells has long been recognized.
claims.source: CNS-site-specificity in immune responses to viral infections and in mechanisms of the non-cytolytic clearance of the virus from non-renewable neurons by T and B cells has long been recognized (Griffin, 2011; Griffin, 2003; Binder and Griffin, 2001; Cho et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies that have established CNS-site-specificity in immune responses.

claims.claim: Less than 1% of infected people develop neuroinvasive disease after natural mosquito-borne or iatrogenic blood-borne exposure to WNV.
claims.source: Indeed, less than 1% of infected people develop neuroinvasive disease after natural mosquito-borne or iatrogenic blood-borne exposure to WNV (Sejvar, 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sejvar, 2016, which provides published evidence for the incidence of WNV neuroinvasive disease.

claims.claim: The intracerebral NHP model of WNV-ND closely mimics WNV neuroinvasive disease in humans in respect to the gradient in severity of affected CNS structures, neuropathology, and ensuing signs of neurological impairment.
claims.source: Nonetheless, we previously showed that the intracerebral NHP model of WNV-ND closely mimics WNV neuroinvasive disease in humans in respect to the (i) gradient in severity of affected CNS structures, (ii) neuropathology, and (iii) ensuing signs of neurological impairment (Maximova et al., 2014), making this model indispensable for studies of disease neuropathogenesis and testing therapeutics and vaccine safety.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Maximova et al., 2014, which provides published evidence for the validity of the NHP model.

claims.claim: Age-related alterations in immune responses are the most well-defined risk factors for increased susceptibility to severe WNV-ND.
claims.source: Besides an immunocompromised state, age-related alterations in immune responses are the most well-defined risk factors for increased susceptibility to severe WNV-ND (Montgomery, 2017), but how changes associated with aging may influence regulation of the immune-neural-synaptic axis in elderly with WNV-ND warrants further investigation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Montgomery, 2017, which provides published evidence for age as a risk factor for WNV-ND.

claims.claim: Peripheral inoculation of immunodeficient or aged NHPs does not result in WNV-ND even with very high doses of WNV.
claims.source: Peripheral inoculation of immunodeficient or aged NHPs does not result in WNV-ND even with very high doses of WNV (Wertheimer et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wertheimer et al., 2010, which provides published evidence for the lack of WNV-ND in peripherally inoculated immunodeficient or aged NHPs.

claims.claim: The rapid course of WNV-ND in the NHP model is consistent with limited data showing that acute WNV encephalitis in NHPs leads to death or a moribund state that requires euthanasia 9–15 days after infection.
claims.source: The rapid course of WNV-ND in our NHP model is consistent with limited data showing that acute WNV encephalitis in NHPs leads to death or a moribund state that requires euthanasia 9–15 days after infection (Arroyo et al., 2004; Pogodina et al., 1983).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Arroyo et al., 2004 and Pogodina et al., 1983, which provide published evidence for the course of WNV encephalitis in NHPs.

claims.claim: A non-fatal encephalitis in NHPs, possibly associated with immunosuppression, can take a subacute course followed by virus persistence.
claims.source: However, a non-fatal encephalitis in NHPs, possibly associated with immunosuppression, can take a subacute course followed by virus persistence (Pogodina et al., 1983).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pogodina et al., 1983, which provides published evidence for subacute WNV encephalitis in NHPs.

claims.claim: Many immune molecules in the neuron-microglia-astrocyte-T-cell axes have been implicated in synaptic pruning during development or pathological elimination/loss of synapses during disease.
claims.source: Many immune molecules in the neuron-microglia-astrocyte-T-cell axes have been implicated in synaptic pruning during development or pathological elimination/loss of synapses during disease, depending on the neuronal network (Perry and O'Connor, 2008; Eroglu and Barres, 2010; Verkhratsky and Nedergaard, 2014; Chung et al., 2013; Tröscher et al., 2019; Kreutzfeldt et al., 2013; Di Liberto et al., 2018; Stephan et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies that have implicated immune molecules in synaptic pruning.

claims.claim: Synaptic elimination in the hippocampus by a complement-microglial axis with assistance of T cells has been proposed as an underlying mechanism of flavivirus-associated cognitive dysfunction in a murine model.
claims.source: Synaptic elimination in the hippocampus by a complement-microglial axis (Vasek et al., 2016) with assistance of T cells (Garber et al., 2019) has also been proposed as an underlying mechanism of flavivirus-associated cognitive dysfunction in a murine model.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Vasek et al., 2016 and Garber et al., 2019, which provide published evidence for synaptic elimination mechanisms in flavivirus infection.

claims.claim: Pleiotropy describes a concept where one gene and its encoded protein can control disparate, apparently unrelated biological processes.
claims.source: Pleiotropy describes a concept where one gene and its encoded protein can control disparate, apparently unrelated BPs (Radisky et al., 2009; Boulanger, 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Radisky et al., 2009 and Boulanger, 2009, which provide published evidence for the concept of pleiotropy.

claims.claim: Many proteins with established functions in the immune system are also expressed in the developing and adult nervous system.
claims.source: Many proteins with established functions in the immune system are also expressed in the developing and adult nervous system.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about protein expression in the immune and nervous systems.

claims.claim: Some pleiotropic proteins such as proinflammatory cytokines and proteins in the complement system and major histocompatibility complex are essential for the establishment, organization, function, and removal of synapses between neurons.
claims.source: Remarkably, some pleiotropic proteins such as proinflammatory cytokines and proteins in the complement system and major histocompatibility complex are essential for the establishment, organization, function, and removal of synapses between neurons (Boulanger, 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Boulanger, 2009, which provides published evidence for the role of pleiotropic proteins in synapse biology.

results.result: WNV infection in humans causes significant morbidity and mortality, with an estimated 7 million people affected in the US since 1999. WNV-ND presents with high in-hospital mortality, motor and cognitive impairment, and increased risk of death during convalescence, yet current treatment remains only supportive.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C8 are all supported by appropriate citations to published literature (Ronca et al., 2019; Davis et al., 2006; Yeung et al., 2017; Kleinschmidt-DeMasters and Beckham, 2015; Patel et al., 2015; Philpott et al., 2019; Sejvar, 2016; Betsem et al., 2017; Vanichanan et al., 2016). These claims establish the epidemiological and clinical context for the study and are well-documented in prior work.

results.result: Prior work has established that WNV can infect the CNS, spread trans-synaptically, and that synaptic loss may underlie cognitive impairment. The impact of WNV infection on neurophysiology is expected to be CNS-region-specific, but understanding of molecular mechanisms underlying CNS regulation during WNV-ND remains incomplete.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C81, C82, and C84 are supported by appropriate citations to published literature. Claims C10 and C83 represent logical inferences based on established knowledge of CNS organization and WNV pathogenesis. Together, these claims establish the rationale and knowledge gaps that motivate the current study.

results.result: The study used CNS tissue samples from NHPs inoculated intracerebrally with wild-type WNV (NY99), with cerebellum and spinal cord selected based on high viral burden, severe histopathological changes, and neurological signs consistent with the function of these structures.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C12 describe the experimental design and sample selection rationale, supported by citations to prior work (Maximova et al., 2014; Maximova et al., 2016) and consistency with human WNV-ND data. The rationale for tissue selection is clearly articulated and well-justified.

results.result: At the presymptomatic stage (3 dpi), no genes were significantly differentially expressed in the cerebellum, while six genes (MX1, IFIT3, IFI44L, PARP9, STAT1, TRIM22) were significantly upregulated in the spinal cord. These genes have dual immune-neural functionality, with MX1 and STAT1 annotated to both immune response and nervous system terms.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C16 are supported by microarray data with appropriate statistical thresholds (FDR < 0.05, fold change ≥2) and gene ontology annotation analysis. The identification of dual-function genes at the presymptomatic stage provides early evidence for the pleiotropic gene regulation that becomes a major theme of the study.

results.result: Gene expression changes were progressive and CNS-region-specific during symptomatic stages of WNV-ND. At 7 dpi, more genes were upregulated than downregulated in both regions, with stronger changes in the spinal cord. At 9 dpi, the spinal cord had about twice as many DEGs as the cerebellum and consistently showed a higher percentage of downregulated genes. Overlap between regions was higher for upregulated (40-42%) than downregulated (9-12%) genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C21 are supported by microarray data and visualized in Figures 1e-h. The progressive, region-specific nature of transcriptional changes is clearly demonstrated. The higher overlap in upregulated genes suggests common immune responses, while lower overlap in downregulated genes suggests region-specific neural dysfunction.

results.result: Overrepresentation testing identified the immune system as the top biological system enriched for upregulated genes and the nervous system for downregulated genes. Upregulated genes were enriched for immune system development, wound healing, and gliogenesis, while downregulated genes were enriched for neuronal development and axon guidance. Analysis of axon growth-modulating molecules suggested a trend toward a permissive rather than inhibitory environment for axonal regeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C28 are supported by overrepresentation testing (FDR < 0.05) and gene ontology enrichment analysis using gProfiler, with visualization in Figures 1g-h and 2a-e. The analysis of 22 axon growth genes (C28) provides mechanistic insight, though the interpretation as 'permissive' is somewhat inferential and would benefit from functional validation.

results.result: Reactome pathway analysis revealed that major immune system subdomains (innate immunity, cytokine signaling, adaptive immunity) were significantly enriched in both cerebellum and spinal cord at symptomatic stages. MAP kinase activation was significant only in the spinal cord at 9 dpi. For the neuronal system, transmission across chemical synapses was commonly affected, with protein-protein interactions at synapses reaching significance only in the spinal cord at 9 dpi.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C33 are supported by Reactome pathway enrichment analysis with visualization in Figures 3c-j. The identification of region-specific differences (MAP kinase activation, protein-protein interactions at synapses) alongside common pathways provides important insights into CNS-region-specific responses to WNV infection.

results.result: Statistical functional enrichment analysis revealed coordinated transcriptional shifts of different magnitudes: large shifts associated with immune responses (host defense, innate/adaptive immunity) and subtle shifts associated with neuronal compartments (cell body, dendrite, axon, synapses) and functions (synaptic transmission, neurotransmitter secretion, synapse organization).
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C35 are supported by statistical functional enrichment analysis using PANTHER (Mi et al., 2019) with visualization in Figures 4a-h. This analysis provides important insight into the relative magnitude of immune versus neural transcriptional dysregulation, with the subtle but coordinated shifts in neural genes being particularly significant for understanding pathogenesis.

results.result: Cell death processes in WNV-ND were regulated bi-directionally, with negative regulation appearing to outweigh positive regulation. Regulation of necroptosis, apoptosis, and necrosis was enriched in neurons and lymphocytes. The magnitude of neuron death regulation was about half that of lymphocyte apoptosis regulation. Lymphocyte apoptosis regulation was region-specific: T cells in cerebellum, B cells in spinal cord.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C42 are supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis (FDR < 0.05) using gProfiler, with visualization in Figures 5a-c. The finding that neuronal cell death regulation is less prominent than lymphocyte apoptosis regulation (C41) is particularly important, as it challenges the assumption that neuronal death is the primary pathogenic mechanism. The region-specific lymphocyte apoptosis patterns (C42) are intriguing and well-supported.

results.result: Immunohistochemistry revealed reactive astrocytosis (GFAP+), microglial/macrophage activation (CD68+), and lymphocytic infiltration (CD20+, CD4+, CD8+) in WNV-infected cerebellum and spinal cord. CD20 B cells and CD4 T cells showed limited parenchymal migration, while CD8 T cells displayed extensive parenchymal infiltration with neuron-centripetal migration and perineuronal topology.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C48 are supported by immunohistochemistry data with visualization in Figure 6a-c. The differential migration patterns of lymphocyte subtypes (C46-C48) are well-documented and provide important insights into cellular immune responses. The neuron-centripetal migration and perineuronal topology of CD8 T cells is particularly striking and well-illustrated.

results.result: WNV antigens were detected in Purkinje cells (cerebellum) and spinal motor neurons. WNV-infected neurons showed markedly reduced immunoreactivity for cell-type-specific markers (CALB in Purkinje cells, ChAT in spinal motor neurons). In spinal motor neurons, ChAT+ cholinergic C-boutons almost completely disappeared, with focal WNV accumulations adjacent to remaining boutons suggesting trans-synaptic spread.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C54 are supported by immunohistochemistry and double immunofluorescent staining with visualization in Figures 7a-d. The loss of cell-type-specific markers in infected neurons (C50-C52) and the near-complete disappearance of C-boutons (C53) provide strong evidence for disruption of neuronal integrity and function. The suggestion of trans-synaptic spread (C54) is reasonable but remains inferential.

results.result: Immunoreactivity for synaptophysin (SYP) and MAP2 was greatly reduced in WNV-infected cerebellum and spinal cord, indicating loss of presynaptic and somatodendritic integrity. Gene ontology analysis identified the synapse as the most significantly dysregulated neuronal compartment, with the spinal cord having 2.5 times more dysregulated synaptic genes than the cerebellum. Both glutamatergic and GABA-ergic synapses were significantly dysregulated.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C59 are supported by immunohistochemistry (Figures 8a-d) and gene ontology enrichment analysis (Figures 8e-f). The convergence of protein-level (reduced SYP and MAP2) and transcriptional-level (GO enrichment) evidence for synaptic dysregulation is particularly compelling. The identification of the synapse as the most dysregulated compartment (C57) is a key finding.

results.result: SynGO analysis revealed extensive synaptic dysregulation in both cerebellum and spinal cord. In the cerebellum, the postsynapse was most affected, with functions including synapse organization and trans-synaptic signaling. The spinal cord had more extensive dysregulation affecting both pre- and postsynaptic locations and functions. At 7 dpi, 80% of cerebellar synaptic genes were upregulated (postsynaptic) while 20% were downregulated (presynaptic). At 9 dpi, downregulated genes increased, with 71.5% downregulated in spinal cord.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C66 are supported by SynGO enrichment analysis with high stringency settings and visualization in Figures 9c-f and Table 2-3. The temporal progression from predominantly upregulated to predominantly downregulated synaptic genes (C62-C66) provides important insights into disease progression. The greater extent of dysregulation in spinal cord versus cerebellum is consistent with other findings in the study.

results.result: Analysis of immune-neural pleiotropic genes revealed that 94 and 179 such genes were induced in cerebellum and spinal cord, respectively. These pleiotropic genes regulate neuronal compartments (somatodendritic, neuron projection, synapse) and functions (neuron projection development, neuron death regulation, synapse structure/activity, synapse pruning). A subset of 36 immune-neural-synaptic pleiotropic genes was identified, including C1QA. Both up- and downregulated pleiotropic genes had functionality in synapse organization at pre- and postsynapses, with upregulated genes enriched for chemical synaptic transmission and downregulated genes enriched for protein catabolic processes at the postsynapse.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C76 are supported by Venn diagram analysis, overrepresentation testing (FDR < 0.05), and SynGO enrichment analysis with visualization in Figures 10a-g and Table 4. The identification of pleiotropic genes with triple immune-neural-synaptic functionality (C72-C76) is a major conceptual advance. The specific identification of C1QA (C73) as a pleiotropic gene with roles in immune response, glial response, neuron differentiation, and synaptic pruning is particularly significant.

results.result: qPCR validation of select transcripts confirmed their significant dysregulation during WNV infection in NHP cerebella. Linear regression analysis showed strong and significant correlations between microarray and qPCR expression values at symptomatic stages (R² = 0.998 at 7 dpi, R² = 0.987 at 9 dpi, p<0.05).
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C78 are supported by qPCR validation data in Supplementary file 10 and linear regression analysis. The high R² values and statistical significance provide strong validation of the microarray results. This technical validation strengthens confidence in all transcriptome-based findings.

results.result: The study's major conclusion is that WNV infection disrupts the homeostasis of the immune-neural-synaptic axis via induction of pleiotropic genes with distinct functions in each component of the axis. This pleiotropic gene regulation suggests an unintended off-target negative impact of virus-induced immune responses on neurotransmission, which may be a common feature of various viral CNS infections.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C80 represent the study's main conclusions, supported by multiple converging lines of evidence including transcriptomics, pathway analysis, immunohistochemistry, and identification of pleiotropic genes. The concept of 'unintended off-target effects' (C80) is a reasonable inference from the data, though the speculation that this may be common to other viral CNS infections requires further investigation. The overall conclusion is well-supported by the comprehensive dataset.

results.result: The Discussion contextualizes the findings by noting that viral replication kinetics were similar in cerebellum and spinal cord, suggesting that differences in transcriptional responses reflect CNS-site-specific host responses rather than differences in viral replication. The intracerebral NHP model closely mimics human WNV-ND despite bypassing peripheral infection, and age-related immune alterations are important risk factors for severe disease.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C92 are supported by citations to prior work (Maximova et al., 2014; Maximova et al., 2016; Griffin, 2011; Sejvar, 2016; Montgomery, 2017; Wertheimer et al., 2010; Arroyo et al., 2004; Pogodina et al., 1983). These claims provide important context for interpreting the study's findings and acknowledge limitations of the model. The discussion of CNS-site-specificity (C86) is particularly important for understanding the regional differences observed.

results.result: The Discussion places the findings in the context of prior work on immune molecules in synaptic pruning and the concept of pleiotropy. Many immune molecules in neuron-microglia-astrocyte-T-cell axes have been implicated in synaptic pruning during development or disease. Pleiotropic proteins such as proinflammatory cytokines and complement proteins are essential for synapse establishment, organization, function, and removal.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C97 are supported by citations to relevant literature (Perry and O'Connor, 2008; Eroglu and Barres, 2010; Vasek et al., 2016; Garber et al., 2019; Radisky et al., 2009; Boulanger, 2009). These claims establish the conceptual framework for interpreting the study's findings on pleiotropic gene regulation and connect the current work to established principles in neuroimmunology.
